strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem articulation: The paper insightfully distinguishes recommendation continual learning from other domains, observing that outdated preferences should be forgotten rather than preserved. The empirical evidence (Table 1) compellingly demonstrates why cumulative LoRA fails for recommendation.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple datasets, extensive ablations (design choices, regularizer variants, hyperparameter sensitivity), multiple metrics, analysis of stability-plasticity via user groups, and distribution shift quantification. Reproducibility details and promised code release support reproducibility.

Solid theoretical analysis: Propositions 1-3 provide direction-wise interpolation interpretation (Corollary 2) and connect softmax-KL to quadratic forms. While not groundbreaking, the theory is technically sound and provides data-aware intuition for the stability-plasticity trade-off.

Consistent empirical improvements: PESO shows 3-9% gains across multiple datasets and metrics (Table 2). Analysis of dormant vs. new users (Table 3) nicely validates the method achieves balanced stability-plasticity in practice.

Practical design with efficiency: The softmax-KL proximal thoughtfully preserves per-module structure. PESO has O(1) storage complexity vs. O(T) for cumulative LoRA with negligible computational overhead.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The core contribution—L2/KL proximal regularization toward previous adapter—applies standard proximal methods. The paper insufficiently clarifies what is novel beyond this well-established technique. The softmax-KL instantiation, while reasonable, lacks novelty.

Theory-practice gap is significant: (1) Theory uses MSE surrogate for cross-entropy loss; (2) linearization is fixed at θ₀ but may not hold as v_t deviates; (3) Assumption 5 (complementarity) is not empirically analyzed; (4) No convergence guarantees or sample complexity bounds. Proposition 1's result (generalized eigenvalue interpolation) is standard and yields limited actionable insights.

Modest and unvalidated empirical gains: Average improvements are 3.71-6.26% without statistical significance testing or confidence intervals. No clear evidence the gains are practically significant (e.g., Table 3: 0.0170 vs. 0.0164 is ~3.7%).

Experimental limitations reduce confidence: (1) Small scale (Llama 3.2 1B; generalization to 7B/70B unclear); (2) E-commerce-centric data (Yelp in appendix); (3) Artificial sparsity (0.9998); (4) λ tuned per dataset without cross-dataset ablation; (5) High sensitivity to learning rate (Figure 4) not fully addressed; (6) No statistical significance testing.

Insufficient analysis of method effectiveness: Why is proximal regularization the right mechanism (vs. replay, orthogonal projection)? Figure 2 shows orthogonality performs worse, but fair comparison unclear. Table 12 shows PESO has higher forgetting on D₁—when is this acceptable? Missing: visualization of learned directions, sensitivity to number of stages T.

Narrow application scope and concerning baseline gap: Only next-item recommendation in sequence generation paradigm. Table 6 shows traditional two-tower methods achieve larger relative gains from continual methods—potential disadvantage for LLM-based approach not addressed.

Missing implementation and evaluation details: Exact architecture specs, beam search constraints, learning rate scheduling, computational cost (wall-clock time, FLOPs) not compared. Sensitivity to sliding window size (20) not analyzed. Why average D₂-D₄ only, excluding D₅?

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly articulates how continual recommendation differs from other domains (vision), showing cumulative LoRA is ill-suited for evolving preferences
Strong empirical motivation: Table 1 convincingly demonstrates cumulative LoRA fails in chronological settings vs. user-disjoint splits
Comprehensive experiments: Multiple datasets, extensive baselines, additional architectures (LC-REC), non-e-commerce data (Yelp), user group analysis (dormant/new users)
Theoretical contribution: Propositions 1-3 provide formal analysis with intuitive p-weighted variance interpretation for softmax-KL proximal
Consistent improvements: Achieves 3-6% gains across datasets, metrics, and architectures with detailed experimental setup and reproducibility commitment
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core contribution (proximal regularizer anchoring to previous state) is straightforward application of standard regularization techniques; methodologically incremental

Theoretical limitations: Linearization assumption (v=0) may not hold for large accumulated updates; Proposition 1's interpolation result follows directly from standard optimization; gap between theoretical p-weighted variance and empirical softmax-KL superiority unclear
Modest improvements without rigor: 3-6% gains lack statistical significance testing (no error bars, confidence intervals, multiple runs); single model size (Llama-3.2 1B) tested

Hyperparameter tuning burden: Requires dataset-specific λ tuning [0.5-8.0] and learning rate scaling (0.05-0.1×); unfair comparison if baselines not equivalently tuned; no principled guidance provided

Incomplete methodological justification: Why explicit proximal regularization when learning rate and gradient dynamics could naturally balance stability-plasticity? Initialization sensitivity (vt←vt-1) not ablated

Limited scope and generalizability: Only next-item recommendation on similar datasets (Amazon categories + Yelp; all e-commerce/location-based); unclear transfer to other continual learning scenarios or LLM paradigms

Concerning findings unexplored: Table 6 shows traditional methods (PISA) achieve larger relative gains than PESO, suggesting fundamental LLM limitations PESO doesn't address; comparison between LLM vs. two-tower approaches underdeveloped

Incomplete analysis: Distribution shift (Table 7) reported but connection to PESO benefits vague; no analysis of performance scaling with drift magnitude; limited ablations on λ consistency, block-diagonal structure, forgetting trade-off (Table 12)

strengths: Clear and novel problem framing: Identifies genuine distinction between continual recommendation and other continual learning domains (vision, graphs); shows stability-plasticity have different meanings in recommendation context

Solid theoretical analysis: Proposition 1 provides elegant generalized-eigen interpolation; Corollary 2 gives clean intuition about data-aware direction-wise balance; Proposition 3 connects softmax-KL to p-weighted variance with clear interpretation
Valuable ablation in Section 3: Systematic comparison of LoRA variants (Table 1) on both natural and user-disjoint splits directly validates why cumulative LoRA fails for continual recommendation

Clever empirical analysis: User group stratification (Table 3) for testing stability (dormant users) vs. plasticity (new users) is effective; distribution shift quantification (Table 7) validates task setup
Practical efficiency: O(1) storage complexity vs. O(T) for cumulative LoRA; negligible computational overhead; modular and easy to implement
Comprehensive experimental coverage: Multiple baseline comparisons (SumLoRA, SD-LoRA, InfLoRA, traditional methods); additional experiments in appendix (LC-REC backbone, Yelp, O-LoRA/AM-LoRA/LSAT)
Well-organized presentation: Clear motivation, good visualization (Figure 1), rigorous proofs, extensive appendix
weaknesses: Modest and unvalidated empirical gains: 0-8.66% improvements with most gains in 1-3% range; no statistical significance testing (no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs); 0.97% improvement on Books NDCG@5 raises questions about practical significance

Restrictive theoretical assumptions: Linearization fixed at θ₀ without empirical validation; quadratic approximation to cross-entropy via MSE surrogate regime not characterized; Assumption 5 (no doubly-flat directions) never verified empirically; large LLMs may operate far from linearization point

Limited experimental scope: All main experiments on Amazon Reviews (3-4 categories) with single Yelp addition; only Llama-3.2 1B backbone; incremental blocks only 10-15% of base data; only 5 evaluation stages

Weak case for LLM-based approach: Traditional two-tower methods (Table 6) are competitive; PISA (traditional) achieves ~29% relative gain vs. PESO's ~6%, undermining value proposition of LLM-based continual recommendation

Design choices inadequately justified: Softmax-KL only marginally better than L2 proximal (Figure 2); Per-Rank KL comparable to softmax-KL; module-level grouping arbitrary; λ selection lacks principled approach despite dataset-dependent values (2.0 vs. 5.0)

Major practical limitations: Fixed item tokenizer prevents handling new items in later stages; no new user cold-start solutions; no principled hyperparameter selection during continual learning without access to future data

Insufficient forgetting analysis: PESO shows higher performance drop on D₁ (0.0107) vs. cumulative LoRA (0.0062); claim that forgetting is 'benign' lacks justification; when would stronger stability be required?
Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite small improvements; unclear if gains exceed noise; only 5 stages of evaluation for 4-5 metrics
